comments.text:
There are MANY factors conspiring to kill the restaurant business. Each of the segments has a unique combination of challenges. The pandemic really broke the patterns that were holding it all together. There are still high quality "fine dining options" but you sort of have to know who is who and what is what. And for those options, where they really are direct sourcing fresh and quality ingredients and keeping professional staff, it is expensive and cost will reflect that. Indeed it is gotten so expensive that it has killed off the occasional event crowds which were basically the profit margin for many such establishments. 

So you do not have many options that are a value proposition and you don't have many options that are high end. Compounding that, urban environments where the traffic required to survive exists now have rents eating past margins, and loss of traditional work lunch crowds. There just isn't a great model that works toady short of exclusive captive customer base locations like major tourist towns and given how that space is managed, the cuisine is generally going to be corproratized and uninspired. Even surviving brick and mortar are moving significant volume via delivery. 

I really miss the pre-pandemic (and more so early 2000's) restaurant days. A lot of friends were in that space and I have been watching it erode over the past decades. Sadly, its a change in social norms at the root which really makes restaurant math impossible today. Tight margins cannot accommodate even a modest demand decline. And the days of big city high end servers being able to make 1% money have faded away so professionals are few and far between today.
